method: Selected primary and contextual sources actually opened during the focused reassessment. Failed openings, unrelated roll calls and automated retrieval without substantive passages are not asserted as verified evidence. Retained subject-specific dossiers remain the principal context; precise new responses are educated assumptions.

source.title: Message to Congress on America's Agenda for the Future: justice, privacy and personal freedoms
source.publisher: Ronald Reagan Presidential Library / National Archives

sources.finding: The justice section pairs forceful lawful enforcement with constitutional rights and protection against improper government intrusion. It also proposes narrower habeas appeals and exclusionary-rule changes, important counter-evidence to absolute opposition to coercive enforcement. It does not give an exact answer to bulk records or compulsory papers.

source.title: Bill of Rights: First, Fourth and Fifth Amendments

sources.finding: The text protects speech and assembly, requires justified searches and provides due process. It is a constitutional framework, not proof that every current executive action complies or that all warrants are required in emergencies.

source.title: NSA operating authorities: intelligence and communications records

sources.finding: The authority overview distinguishes foreign intelligence, targeted acquisition and the historical bulk telephone metadata programme. Metadata is not communications content. Historical descriptions are not treated as proof that a discontinued programme still operates; separate subject periods and retained reforms are considered.

source.title: Senate roll call 148: amendment to prohibit warrantless access to US persons' communications

sources.finding: Rubio voted Nay on the Durbin warrant-access amendment. This is earlier-period contextual evidence, not an exact vote on the revised bulk-records question or proof of a fresh 2025–2026 policy. Vance was Not Voting, which supplies no affirmative or negative policy response for him.

source.title: Trump, Vance and Musk take aim at courts reviewing executive actions

sources.finding: Reports challenges to judicial oversight and claims about legitimate executive discretion. This is counter-evidence to uniformly strong support for judicial remedies, but the reported disputes are not themselves a complete personal policy on movement restrictions. The exact new scenario remains inferred.

source.title: Border Patrol monitoring of US drivers and travel-pattern-based stops

sources.finding: Actual tracking and stops are counter-evidence to an absolute absence of intrusive police practice. Border and immigration powers are distinct from unrestricted general searches or universal identity-paper duties. The report does not establish that every ordinary adult encounter has the same legal rules.

source.title: Countering Domestic Terrorism and Organized Political Violence

sources.finding: The order directs investigation of funding and NGOs linked to alleged criminal activity. That is not a literal blanket requirement of permission to form peaceful civic groups. It is considered alongside retained speech/association commitments as a conditional coercion concern, rather than equating peaceful organisation with terrorism.

source.title: Bulk acquisition of communications data: code of practice

sources.finding: The official publication concerns genuine bulk acquisition powers, with legal authorisation and oversight. It is used as institutional context for the relevant governing periods, not as proof that a later code was enacted by every earlier leader. Broad acquisition differs from targeted interception even when each has safeguards.

source.title: Police stop and search powers and rights

sources.finding: The guidance distinguishes ordinary grounds from authorised suspicionless area powers. Being asked questions is not itself a general duty to carry identification. Defined area powers explain qualified agreement on searches outside an immediate emergency rather than unlimited ordinary police discretion.

source.title: Compulsory identification: limits and purposes of police requests

sources.finding: Police requests require a reason; public-order and investigation contexts can cover nonsuspects. Inability to show accepted identity documents can bring penalties. This supports qualified agreement, not unrestricted arbitrary requests or treating identification duties as unlimited carrying powers.

source.title: Is a national identity card compulsory?

sources.finding: Official guidance says no text obliges possession of a national identity card. Identity checks and proof in particular transactions remain possible. That distinction weighs against the universal carrying formulation without denying actual police identity powers.

source.title: Hiibel: US government brief on identity during a justified investigative stop

sources.finding: The government's argument concerns identifying a suspect during an investigative stop, not every adult carrying documents. A litigant's brief is not a Supreme Court holding; the retained constitutional and search-case dossier supplies the complementary framework.

source.title: Libertarian Party platform: individual privacy and civil freedoms

sources.finding: The programme supports individual privacy and opposition to governmental coercion. It provides context for the retained specific libertarian school; it is not substituted for other ideologies or for a personality simply sharing a libertarian label.

source.title: South African Constitution, Chapter 2: Bill of Rights

sources.finding: The framework protects personal security, privacy and peaceful association with legal remedies. It is period-relevant to the Mandela settlement, but does not establish every later enforcement practice or prohibit every specifically authorised security search.

source.title: Identity Cards Act 2006 explanatory notes, section 13 paragraph 95

sources.finding: Paragraph 95 expressly excludes compulsory carrying and production on demand under section 13, except in the public-service application context. Supporting the identification scheme is not evidence of supporting universal police carrying/showing obligations.

source.title: Executive Order 12333: original 1981 intelligence activities order
source.publisher: Ronald Reagan Presidential Library / National Archives

sources.finding: The original order supports vigorous intelligence collection including international terrorism and narcotics, but states constitutional constraints and differentiated restrictions on US-person information and domestic techniques. It is counter-evidence to uniform opposition to intelligence, while not establishing support for the new general bulk crime-records permission or the later amended digital programmes.
